1 Table 1

Table 1 shows the summary distributions of all variables grouped by the treatment. The standardized mean difference (SMD) is also reported to assess the balance of covariates between the two treatment groups. An SMD less than 0.1 is generally considered indicative of good balance. As we can see, many of the baseline variables’SMD exceed 0.1. This is not due to any confounding as the patients were randomized. Thus, what we see is chance imbalance. Take a look, for example, aerobic fitness at baseline. Even though the SMD is near 0.5, the mean and median between SEPA and C-LIFE are very similar. Thus, the high SMD value is due to highly skewed distribution of the variable (SMD is sensitive to skewness). Figure 1 shows the density plot of aerobic fitness at baseline by treatment group. As we can see, the distribution is highly skewed and the mean and median are very similar between the two groups.

We imputed missing data using the covariates, treatment group, and outcome variables. We generated 5 imputed datasets. Most analyses were carried out separately for each dataset to account for uncertainties introduced by imputation.

2 Result

2.1 Average Treatment Effect (ATE)

The primary outcome of interest has been chosen as a memory as it showed the largest average treatment effect.

We assessed convergence of BCF model using Gelman-Rubin’s convergence diagnostic and the time-series standard error for the square root of the residual variance parameter, \(\sigma\), since this parameter often mixes slowly in tree-based MCMC1. For \(\sigma\), the Gelman-Rubin statistic was slighly above 1.01 in each imputed dataset, which suggests some remaining autocorrelation or lack of perfect missing. However, this does not by itself mean the MCMC run is unusable.

To gauge the practical size of Monte Carlo error, we compared the time-series standard error to the posterior standard deviation of \(\sigma\). Across all five imputed datasets, the time-series standard error was about 2% of the posterior SD, indicating that Monte Carlo error is small relative to the posterior uncertainty. In other words, the posterior spread in \(\sigma\) reflects genuine uncertainty from the data and model, not primarily simulation error from an insufficient MCMC run.

The slightly elevated Gelman–Rubin values therefore indicate that additional sampling could improve mixing, but the current draws already appear precise enough for summarizing \(\sigma\). We would still check that the primary causal estimands, such as the ATE and subgroup ATEs, also have acceptable ESS and Gelman–Rubin diagnostics.

The posterior median and 95% credible intervals of the parameters are shown in Table 2:

The posterior median (95% credible interval) for average treatment effect (${}) is $ 0.266 (-5.612, 6.803), which suggest potential positive effect of the treatment on memory. However, the credible interval includes the null value of zero, thus, the evidence of treatment effect is not strong. In addition, the ATE signal is relatively small compared to the residual noise (\(\sigma =\) 13.560 (9.753, 17.500)), suggesting that the treatment effects are hard to estimate precisely.

2.2 Average Treatment Effect by Age and Gender

Age (\(\leq 60\) vs. \(> 60\)) and gender (Male vs. Female) were pre-determined by the PI to be a potential effect modifier. We assessed the treatment effect by age and gender.

2.3 Identifying Potential Subgroup

The root split was on Mean ambulatory DBP at baseline. On average, patients with Mean ambulatory DBP at baseline less than 66 showed negative effect of the treatment, while those with Mean ambulatory DBP at baseline \(\geq 66\) showed positive effect of the treatment. Among observations Mean ambulatory DBP at baseline \(\geq 66\), the next split was on Memory at baseline. Among the observations Mean ambulatory DBP at baseline \(< 66\), the next split was on Clinic DBP baseline. (After pruning using the 1-SE rule, some lower-level splits, such as the split on Baseline stroke risk score using Framingham (without age), were removed, indicating that those subtrees did not improve cross-validated prediction enough to justify their additional complexity.). Please note that adbasT1 refers to Baseline brachial artery diameter.
